summary: One of the set of documents describing the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), an application-level protocol for distributed printing. This one sets out requirements for notifications in IPP.

eli5.summary: A wish list of what printer notices should be able to do, written before designing them.

subtitle: A wish list for how printers should tell people and programs about jobs and printer events.

tldr.problem: Users, operators and programs want to hear when a print job finishes or a printer changes state, but IPP had no standard way to ask for or deliver such notices.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines terms, walks through 12 scenarios and sets out 17 requirements that a future IPP notification specification must meet, for example subscriptions, delivery methods and localization.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. The actual extensions are defined elsewhere, and the memo points to RFC 3995.

today: RFC 3997 is an Informational requirements memo and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. The extensions that address it are described in RFC 3995.

sections.title: Scope and Context
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing on the Internet. Its primary architectural components are the Model, the Protocol and an interface to Directory Services. This document is one of a set describing IPP, and it states the requirements for notifications as an optional part of an IPP service.

The scope covers three kinds of IPP users: End Users, Print Administrators and Operators. The extensions that meet these requirements are described in RFC 3995, which extends IPP/1.0, IPP/1.1 and future versions.
sections.eli5: IPP lets people print over the network. This memo is about how a printer should tell people what is happening with their print job.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The memo defines 24 terms. The roles include the Job-Submitting End User, Administrator, Operator, Job Recipient and Job Recipient Proxy (someone who picks up the printout on the recipient's behalf). A Notification Subscriber asks the printer to send notices, and a Notification Recipient receives them, possibly through a Notification Recipient Agent.

An Event is a change of state, condition or configuration of a Job or Printer object. An Event Notification is generated when one occurs and is delivered only if a matching subscription exists, using the delivery method named in it, for example email. Delivery can be immediate or store-and-forward. Reliable delivery needs both store-and-forward and a reliable transport. A notification can be human-consumable, machine-consumable or mixed.
sections.eli5: Someone asks the printer to ring a bell, and when something happens the printer tells whoever they named, by the way they chose, like a text or an email.

sections.title: Scenarios
sections.content:
Twelve scenarios illustrate what people need. A user down the hall wants an immediate notice with the job state reasons. A user working from home wants an immediate notice sent to a secretary and a store-and-forward email to themselves. Others print to a client's printer in Belgium with notices in French, or to a print shop and check by email in the morning.

Further scenarios cover an operator who subscribes independently of any job to follow all Printer state transitions, a usage statistics application that subscribes to job completion, and client programs that keep a job list or printer list up to date and only poll slowly to recover missed notices. The last three describe IPP servers that front devices: one polls devices that cannot send notices, one chooses between forwarding notices or substituting itself as recipient, and one adds a job subscription for itself to a client's subscriptions, which the memo calls piggybacking.
sections.eli5: The memo imagines many situations, such as waiting by the printer, printing at work from home, or a program watching a queue, and asks what notices each one would need.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The 17 requirements apply to the notification specification, not to implementations. The specification must say which requirements are REQUIRED and which are OPTIONAL. It must let a printer use third-party notification services. It must let a job submitter name zero or more recipients and the events each wants, subject to administrative and security policy. Listed events include Job Received, Job Started, Page Complete, Collated Copy Complete, Job Complete, Job Aborted, Job Canceled and device problems.

Users must be able to subscribe to job events for a specific job and, without submitting a job, to printer events for a defined period or to job events for all jobs. Immediate or store-and-forward delivery must be selectable for each recipient, and common delivery methods such as email must be defined. At least one class of delivery methods must flow through corporate firewalls.

A printer that cannot use the requested delivery scheme still accepts the job and reports the unsupported attribute values, and it need not validate the recipient. Human-consumable notices must be localizable. Job-independent subscriptions must not go stale, but must not be dropped merely because of temporary delivery problems. A subscription must be addable to an existing job, cancellable, and listable.
sections.eli5: The wish list says people must be able to choose which events to hear about, who hears, and how, and to change their mind later. The printer should still accept the job even if it cannot send the notice.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The biggest concern is abuse of notification: unwanted notices sent to third parties, in effect spam, made worse when an address is a mailing list. Some scenarios require third-party notification, and the fully secure solution of getting every recipient's agreement conflicts with requirement 9. Some systems may disallow third-party notification, as in the traditional fax model.

Submitting a notification request carries the same security issues as an IPP/1.1 print request, so HTTP authentication and HTTP/TLS privacy can be used. Only the creator or an operator should cancel a subscription, and long-lived subscriptions may be limited to privileged users. Notices should use the delivery method with the strongest security when they are sensitive.

For internationalization, human-consumable notices must be localized to the language and charset the subscriber chooses among those the printer supports. Machine-consumable notices use the application/ipp MIME media type.
sections.eli5: A printer that mails anyone you name could be used to pester people. So the rules say who may sign people up and cancel, and sensitive notices should travel the safest way.
